catechol degradation II (meta-cleavage pathway)

PathwayMech / Browse pathways / MetaCyc:PWY-5420

MetaCyc:PWY-5420

The complete seven-step oxidative catechol meta-cleavage route consists of the four reactions of PWY-5419 followed by the three reactions of PWY-5162. Ring cleavage, NAD-dependent semialdehyde oxidation, tautomerization and enol-producing decarboxylation feed the shared hydration/aldolase/acylating-dehydrogenase tail. Pyruvate branches at aldol cleavage; acetaldehyde continues to acetyl-CoA. The complete formal net transformation consumes catechol, oxygen, two waters, CoA(4−) and two NAD(1−), producing carbon dioxide, pyruvate, acetyl-CoA(4−), two NADH(2−) and three hydrons.

Native formal reaction orientation is kept independently from route traversal and from the six selected directional Rhea equations. Native RXN-8529 is reversible and matches the 28080-to-64908 tautomerization, not its wrong-stereoisomer Rhea32214 cross-reference. Native4.1.1.77-RXN yields the 2Z dienol; linked ketoRhea24261 is not an exact substitute. The hydratase is traversed native right-to-left. Native parent2E prose and historical substrate preparations do not independently establish modern2Z/S stereochemistry.

The four listed taxa are exact native parent species annotations, not four independently demonstrated complete routes. Historical Pseudomonas putida mt-2 remains the source-specific ORG-5948 context without a guessed taxonomy alias. Component donors, broader taxonomic ranges and heterologous expression hosts do not become whole-route taxa. All native activity assignments preserve their evidence classes and preparation limits. Gene nodes retain exact identity context and reciprocal product pointers in the accompanying ledger; no unsupported encodes predicate is invented.

NbaG remains a predicted component; CnbE/F unchlorinated formal promotion is excluded because the described coupled assay is chlorinated. CnbG unchlorinated extract activity is distinct. AP3 decarboxylase gene spelling conflicts across native/UniProt, exact ENA accession/CDS and papers; accession-grounded identity does not resolve the historical AmnF partner or absolute assembly count. Modern engineered8IH6 tagged5+5 is a separate preparation. The native Cu/Hg regulator conflict is explicit. Native XylH six-subunit annotation, historical mass interpretation and modified crystal preparations remain separate. DmpFG is2+2; its native negative NADH sign is excluded in favor of primary-author adjudication. E.coli ADHE-CPLX is explicitly excluded by PWY5162, without excluding unrelated AdhE proteins.

Source-specific enzyme scope follows. These native database descriptions preserve source inference and preparation limits; cited papers are not thereby claimed independently read.

Evidence scope: publisher abstract and reference list only; full-text loading placeholder. Purified pWW0 hydrolase was a two-subunit protein with preferences among ring-fission products. [DOI:10.1099/00221287-132-3-717]

Evidence scope: Scientific main HTML inspected except Table3 homolog catalog; no activity assay, no figure visual claims. The authors use AmnE for AP3 2-aminomuconate deaminase. They lacked AP3 cells, used a synthetic gene and reported no enzyme-activity assay because unstable substrate production failed. Recombinant AmnE was produced in BL21(DE3)pLysS from pET28a; purification included nickel affinity, thrombin tag removal, ion exchange and size exclusion. The 142-residue deaminase structure 6IZH has nine asymmetric-unit protomers; the biological interpretation is a hexamer, supported by an approximately 103.5 kDa solution estimate. R56A and deletion49–59 favored trimers; P126A remained hexameric. These are deaminase assembly experiments, not evidence for decarboxylase/hydratase stoichiometry. [DOI:10.3389/fmicb.2019.02079]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. Coexpressed 4-OD/VPH and E106Q-VPH complexes were purified; the mutant retained decarboxylase but lacked detected hydratase activity. The reported 2,4E label concerns a terminal deuterated double bond; it does not identify C2 E/Z. Enol formation and subsequent VPH-associated ketonization are distinct. Wild-type complex favored a 3S deuterated keto product, while mutant complex gave racemate. The carbon isotope effect supports a proposed late, nearly rate-limiting decarboxylation step. An official correction exists but its content was not obtained. Detailed mechanistic claims remain correction-sensitive; no numeric isotope effects or exact constructs are accepted from the abstract alone. [PMID:10651637]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. The abstract maps purified-enzyme N termini to AmnC dehydrogenase, AmnF deaminase, AmnE decarboxylase and AmnD hydratase. These names conflict with the issuing sequence deposit and later sources. Clustering suggests an operon but is not a transcription experiment. The full paper and its metal/assembly assays remain unavailable; native 300 kDa, 1:1 and Cu/Hg details are source assertions, not primary-verified measurements here. [PMID:11081795]

Evidence scope: complete scientific HTML main text and four visual figures. NbaE/F/G/H/I/J functions are predicted by homology. NbaG decarboxylase is 251 residues in the table; no isolated NbaG activity is reported. Constructs and enzymology characterize NbaC and NbaD, not NbaG. NbaD decarboxylates a different amino-carboxy-semialdehyde substrate. Fe2+ dependence, histidine52/96 mutagenesis and metal inhibition belong to NbaC dioxygenase, not NbaG decarboxylase. AP3 AmnF is identified as hydratase and AmnD as deaminase in comparative sequence context, conflicting with the2000 abstract assignments. Insertions in nbaJ/R/D/F abolish growth on2-nitrobenzoate; gene cluster and possible polar effects do not substitute for NbaG-specific biochemical testing. LysR motifs and insertion phenotype support a proposed regulator; detailed regulation was outside study scope. Keto/enol labels and common downstream machinery are comparative interpretation, not exact2Z orS measurements for KU7. [PMID:12620844]

Evidence scope: partial main text: publisher pages 6992–6993 only, extracted L0–152; remaining 6994–6997 not read. The stated biological unit is a 140 kDa tetramer of two DmpFG heterodimers; eight chains in the asymmetric unit form two biological tetramers. Native and SeMet crystals differ. Three DmpF chains are NAD-bound and one apo despite crystallization with NAD; proposed domain motion and CoA-site interpretation are hypotheses. A 29 Å tunnel supports structural channeling interpretation. Introductory turnover and acetaldehyde Km comparisons were explicitly unpublished data. The biological unit is a tetramer of two DmpFG heterodimers; one heterodimer is a catalytic pair. Crystal conditions and cofactor occupancy differ across subunits. Tunnel geometry supports a structural channeling proposal; cited stimulation and acetaldehyde Km in the introduction were unpublished data. [PMID:12764229]

Evidence scope: complete scientific HTML main text and four visual figures. CnbE is hydratase (279 residues); CnbF is decarboxylase (262 residues). Both are classified as tentative by homology in the abstract and discussion. The caption additionally reports coupled CnbE/CnbF coexpression activity in recombinant E. coli, with data not shown. This is limited experimental support, not isolated-enzyme characterization. Named constructs use BL21(DE3), pET21a except CnbH in pET28a. Table1 supplies CnbG but no CnbE/F construct details. CnbG extract converts unchlorinated 2-hydroxymuconate to a keto product by 296-to236nm spectral shift; empty-vector control is included. Chlorinated tautomerase scope is named, but Figure3 directly tests the unchlorinated substrate. Do not conflate CnbH deaminase activity with CnbG tautomerase. Chlorinated compound numbering/names and CnbI mass/length/function descriptions contain inconsistencies; they do not establish exact modern route chemistry. The paper calls AP3 AmnD the deaminase, conflicting with PMID11081795 abstract D/F assignments. Preserve conflict pending deposit/full primary resolution. Plasmid curing abolishes nitrobenzene/chloronitrobenzene growth. This does not prove the complete catechol PWY5420 route in CNB1; neighboring catA evidence concerns ortho cleavage. CnbR regulation is explicitly unresolved; a putative regulator is not a demonstrated causal regulatory edge. Figure4 labels BAB03536 deaminase as AmnE, while Discussion calls the deaminase AmnD. The paper is internally inconsistent; ENA also labels BAB03536 as AmnE. [PMID:16517619]

Evidence scope: Complete scientific main HTML, four kinetic/stereochemical tables and 20 original graphics inspected; supporting-information contents unavailable.. YwhB from B. subtilis catalyzes several tested enol/dienol ketonizations in vitro. The paper explicitly leaves its biological function unresolved and identifies no genomic context establishing a pathway. P1A and R11A YwhB mutants were overproduced in E. coli BL21(DE3)pLysS and purified to more than 95% homogeneity by the reported SDS-PAGE assessment. Their DNA sequences and expected protein masses were checked. The main report interprets mutant mass spectra as showing the expected products without a retained initiating methionine blocking the first catalytic residue. Mutant labels use processed enzyme positions P1A and R11A. Steady-state assays used 20 mM sodium phosphate, pH 7.3, at 23°C, with spectrophotometric monitoring and nonlinear regression. Table errors are standard deviations. For compound 2→1, YwhB performs 1,3 ketonization of 2-hydroxymuconate to the β,γ-unsaturated keto tautomer, with kcat 10±1 s−1 and Km 76±17 µM under the assay conditions. YwhB also catalyzes compound 2→3, the 1,5 ketonization, with kcat 26.0±1.4 s−1 and Km 940±70 µM; its catalytic efficiency is 2.8±0.2 × 10^4 M−1 s−1. YwhB converts HPD (compound 5) to 2-oxo-4-pentenoate (4) by 1,3 ketonization: kcat 112±14 s−1, Km 243±42 µM and kcat/Km 4.6±0.8 × 10^5 M−1 s−1. YwhB catalyzes 1,3 ketonization of phenylenolpyruvate (7), p-hydroxyphenylenolpyruvate (8) and the seven-carbon dicarboxylate dienol (11); efficiencies differ substantially across these analogues. Only the six-carbon diacid 2 yielded a measurable YwhB 1,5 ketonization rate among the tested dienols. Corresponding α,β-keto formation from 5 and 11 was too close to nonenzymatic rates to measure reliably. P1A and R11A eliminate detectable 2→1 and 2→3 activities under the reported assays. Both retain reduced ketonization of HPD and phenylenolpyruvate; Arg-11 replacement has the larger effect. Table 2 reports HPD Km values of 243±42 µM for wild-type YwhB and 378±100 µM for P1A, an approximately 1.56-fold increase. S15 instead calls it a 1.6-fold decrease. Products generated in D2O were trapped by borohydride reduction and converted through ozonolysis and malic-enzyme treatment to labeled malate. Partial proton NMR spectra were used to assign isotope-dependent stereochemistry. Ketonization of HPD (5) by YwhB in D2O favors (3R)-[3-2H]-2-oxo-4-pentenoate (4) by approximately 4.4:1, inferred from the derivatized malate NMR signals. Phenylenolpyruvate (7) ketonization in D2O favors (3R)-[3-2H]-phenylpyruvate (9) by approximately 3:1 in the reported derivatization/NMR analysis. YwhB ketonization of diacid 2 to compound 1 in D2O favors (3S)-[3-2H]-2-oxo-4-hexenedioate by approximately 8:1, opposite to the favored C-3 configuration for the tested monoacids. Incubating diacid 2 with 4-OT in D2O yielded approximately equal C-3 isotope stereoisomers of keto compound 1. The analysis was repeated with the same result. The YwhB diacid reaction proceeded for 1 min before NaBH4 addition and then 1 h before workup. In the 4-OT comparator, enzyme and NaBH4 were added together and the mixtures stood overnight. After trapping the YwhB diacid reaction, the isolated material contained about 26 mg of reduced compound 1 and 11 mg of reduced compound 3. The 4-OT experiment recovered these reduced products in an approximate 1:2 ratio. Opposite labeled C-3 preferences for monoacids and diacid 2 motivate different substrate orientations involving Arg-11. Pro-1 general-base chemistry and altered charge stabilization are proposed explanations for the mutant effects. The introduction describes YwhB as a hexamer of 61-residue subunits and cites prior structural literature. This study does not newly determine its native oligomerization. The cited 4-OT 2→3 kinetic comparator is kcat 3500 s−1 and Km 180 µM. S14 attributes these values to reference 13, rather than measuring them anew in the YwhB kinetic table. The authors propose that the pathway role of 4-OT may be primarily 2→3 1,5 ketonization, with keto compound 1 interconverting chemically with enol 2. They present this as a revised possibility requiring kinetic discrimination. YwhB had no known biological role or obvious gene context; in-vitro 1,3-tautomerization had higher catalytic efficiency than 1,5 activity, and P1A/R11A impaired these reactions. The newly inspected main text refines the comparison: the favored 1,3 route has higher catalytic efficiency, not higher kcat, and isotope trapping protocols differ. D2O experiments gave predominantly3R products from two monoacids and3S from a diacid; 4-OT gave racemic3-deuterated diacid product. The newly inspected main text refines the comparison: the favored 1,3 route has higher catalytic efficiency, not higher kcat, and isotope trapping protocols differ. [PMID:17902707]

Evidence scope: complete publisher PDF transformed text; all pages, methods, results, discussion, references, legible tables and figure captions read. PKO1 chromosomal donor DNA was assayed mainly in P. aeruginosa PAO1.93 catA clones. Those hosts are not native pathway taxa. Deletion mapping supports tbuE/F/G/K/I/H/J order and corresponding ring-cleavage, hydrolytic, oxidative, aldolase, decarboxylase, tautomerase and hydratase activities. The terminal acylating dehydrogenase was not mapped. tbuS in trans restored repression without inducer and induction with phenol. TbuR concerned the upstream phenol hydroxylase. Direct effector binding and promoter occupancy were model interpretations. Phenol and m-cresol induced extract activities; tested catechols and other cresols did not. Noninduction is not enzyme inhibition or inability to metabolize after induction. Catechol and both methylcatechols were ring-cleavage substrates. Heterologous methylcatechol growth used phenol inducer and was reported without displayed data. Promoter-region deletion abolished downstream activities despite trans regulator complementation. Ring-cleavage-only clones accumulated yellow semialdehyde. The principal genetics and extract assays use PKO1 donor DNA in a heterologous catA host. Hydrolase assays detected formate from catechol ring-cleavage substrate; hydratase and aldolase used synthesized substrates and coupled readouts. Deletion mapping supports one tbu structural operon and its reported gene order. Phenol induction, partial derepression and trans complementation were measured in defined clone combinations. TbuS restored phenol-responsive control in trans; TbuR concerns phenol hydroxylase. Repression without inducer and activation with inducer form the authors model. Phenol and m-cresol induced the measured pathway activities; the other tested aromatics did not under these culture conditions. Clone-expressed catechol2,3-dioxygenase processed catechol and both methylcatechols; induced cells also grew on methylcatechols. Promoter deletion abolished downstream activity even with trans regulatory complementation; ring-cleavage-only clones accumulated yellow semialdehyde. [PMID:1856161]

Evidence scope: Complete scientific main HTML and eight original figures inspected; primer, SDS-PAGE and GC-MS supplements unavailable.. The native source is Paenibacillus sp. JJ-1b, ATCC 35889. PraB/C/D were expressed in E. coli BL21(DE3); this host is an experimental preparation, not another native pathway taxon. PraB was expressed from pETB23: pET21a(+) carrying a 1.9-kb NdeI–HindIII praB fragment. BL21(DE3) cells were induced with 1 mM IPTG at 30°C for 4 h. PraC was expressed from pETC23: pET21a(+) carrying a 0.4-kb NdeI–EcoRI praC fragment. BL21(DE3) cells were induced with 1 mM IPTG at 30°C for 4 h. PraD was expressed from pC4D23: pColdIV carrying a 0.8-kb NdeI–XhoI praD fragment. BL21(DE3) cultures were cooled to 15°C and induced with 0.1 mM IPTG for 24 h. Sonicated cells were centrifuged at 15,000 × g for 15 min; supernatants were used as crude enzyme preparations. Reported PraB rates are per milligram of extract protein, not purified-enzyme turnover numbers. Crude PraB consumes HMS with NAD+ and yields an HMA-assigned product, supported by a 375-to-295-nm spectral change and a reported GC-MS derivative consistent with HMA. Crude PraB activity was 1.19 ± 0.07 U/mg with NAD+ and 0.113 ± 0.009 U/mg with NADP+. NAD+ is preferred by about 11-fold under these conditions; NADP+ also supports measurable activity. Adding crude PraC during the PraB reaction shifts the product spectrum toward 236 nm, supporting HMA-to-OCA tautomerization. Figure 3C displays the rise near 236 nm with loss of the HMS signal. After crude PraD was added to the PraC mixture, an HPD-assigned HPLC peak appeared at 6.03 min after 10 min. Its spectrum peaked at 272 nm; initial OCA/HMA peaks were at 0.89/2.50 min. The PraD assay included 500 µM MgSO4, pH 7.3 Tris buffer and incubation at 35°C. Added magnesium is an explicit experimental condition. PraD activity was measured using its separately expressed crude extract added to a PraA/PraB/PraC-derived mixture; a PraE expression product was not a specified component of this assay. The source distinguishes HMA, keto OCA and enol HPD. Figure 1 draws their proposed structures, while Figure 4 resolves a starting OCA/HMA mixture and the later HPD-assigned product. PraE is assigned HPD hydratase by sequence similarity (52% identity to BphH; 45% to NbaH), with whole-cluster growth and cotranscription supporting its placement downstream of PraD. PraF is assigned HOV aldolase by sequence similarity (58% identity to NahM; 51% to XylK), with whole-cluster growth and cotranscription supporting the downstream role. PraG is assigned the acetaldehyde-to-acetyl-CoA step by sequence similarity (61% identity to NahO; 53% to NbaJ), with whole-cluster growth and cotranscription providing pathway-context support. E. coli BL21(DE3) carrying pBRI23 with praR-praABEGFDCHI acquired growth on M9 medium containing 10 mM 4HB as sole carbon source within 10 days. This supports a functional transferred 4HB catabolic gene set. RT-PCR supports one praABEGFDCHI transcriptional unit and separate praR transcription. Catabolic transcripts were evident after JJ-1b growth on 4HB or PCA and not evident under the reported succinate condition. In E. coli DH5α, a praR-containing praA promoter–lacZ reporter increased activity with 4HB or PCA, while the reporter lacking praR was constitutively active. The result supports PraR-dependent repression. PraA first generates the 350-nm 5CHMS-assigned species, which shifts toward HMS over a longer incubation. PraH accelerates the 350-to-375-nm conversion on the short assay timescale. The experimentally reconstructed entry is 4HB→PCA→5CHMS→HMS, sharing PraB/C/D and inferred PraE/F/G chemistry with a catechol meta-cleavage tail. The study does not establish a catechol ring-cleavage enzyme in JJ-1b. Figure 8 compares pra with xyl, nah and dmp clusters and with predicted clusters in other bacilli. A proposed benzoate transporter appears in the B. licheniformis comparison. The main study supplies no PraB/C/D native oligomer determination or direct catalytic-residue experiment. Homolog identities in Table 2 and automatic sequence annotations must retain their inferential status. Figure 4 is the PraD HPLC product experiment. Figure 5 instead shows PraI conversion of 4HB to PCA; Figure 7 is the PraR reporter and Figure 8 is comparative gene organization. [PMID:19717587]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. Thirteen pWW0 operon genes were ordered by expression mapping. XylG, H, I, J and K assignments support oxidative and shared-tail context. The paper left xylQ and xylT functions unknown. Do not retrospectively cite it as direct seventh-step XylQ proof. Maxicell expression mapping identified thirteen pWW0 operon genes and approximate product masses. [PMID:2183008]

Evidence scope: complete publisher-transformed text, 10 pages; numeric OCR limits; no raw PDF or figures. The purified PaW1/pWW0 enzyme was called benzaldehyde dehydrogenase and attributed to xylC in 1990. Its later N-terminal reassignment to XylG must accompany reuse of these experiments. Benzyl-alcohol/xylene induction, Affi-Gel Blue retention and DTT handling concern this native preparation. They differ from the 1995 KT2440 pWW0-161 experiments. Apparent native/subunit masses were 126/57 kDa, supporting a dimer. A lower native-gel band showed activity after DTT treatment; this is not a universal monomer-activity rule. Benzaldehyde oxidation yielded benzoate and NADH in a 1:1 ratio by HPLC. NADP supported less than 1% of NAD activity at 1 mM; these assays concern benzaldehyde, not HMS. pH 9.6 and pro-R hydride transfer concern benzaldehyde assays. Do not call them HMS optimum or directly measured HMS hydride stereochemistry. Magnesium improved storage stability modestly, while tested salts did not activate aldehyde dehydrogenase. Distinguish storage effects from catalysis and from the separate benzyl-alcohol dehydrogenase. EDTA and phenanthroline did not inhibit in the tested conditions. Thiol reagents inhibited; mercaptoethanol restored pCMB-treated activity. These observations do not identify a particular catalytic residue. The aldehyde dehydrogenase was not apparently inhibited by NADH. Reverse activity with benzoate/NADH was not detected under the tested conditions; ester hydrolysis was an adjacent activity of unclear physiological relevance. [PMID:2202600]

Evidence scope: PubMed original indexed abstract only. E. coli MhpF showed activity as a monomer and catalytic properties independent of oligomeric state. Native acetaldehyde competitive inhibition Ki265000µM is absent from the inspected primary abstract. [PMID:23237860]

Evidence scope: complete scientific main text from publisher transformation; no raw PDF or figures. Native PaW1/pWW0 purification differs from temperature-induced E. coli K-12 single-gene constructs. XylJ alone retained hydratase activity; isolated XylI activity was unstable. Methods reverse H/I gene functions relative to the final interpretation; one Results sentence reverses 27/28 kDa assignments. Use XylH tautomerase, XylI decarboxylase and XylJ hydratase with these conflicts retained. The 28 kDa native/3.5 kDa apparent subunit estimates are historical; the authors acknowledged abnormal SDS mobility. They do not establish an eight-subunit enzyme. Tautomerization and side-activity assays depended on buffer and salts. Six-minute spontaneous conversion was condition-specific; NMR product assignment was personal communication, not a reported experiment. Decarboxylase and hydratase copurified in a preparation near 130 kDa with two polypeptides. Exact subunit copy numbers were not measured. Hydratase favored the freshly prepared enol pool. Aged substrate accumulated resistant keto material and an unidentified degradation product; neither historic names nor absorbance assigns exact E/Z. Decarboxylase used the keto diacid and produced mainly a dienol by spectral estimation. Magnesium dependence and kinetic values belong to those preparations; manganese also accelerated spontaneous conversion. The hydratase product keto/enol form remained explicitly unresolved. The text/figure product-number inconsistency must not silently decide formal chemistry. Native PaW1 purification and recombinant single-component studies used different preparations. Multiple tautomeric chemical forms are distinguished; hydratase monitoring used enol absorbance and separate alkaline total-pool measurement. Methods/function labels and one molecular-mass assignment conflict with the abstract and discussion. Recombinant isomerase purification and uncertain oligomer estimate concern the oxidative branch. Native decarboxylase and hydratase copurified; their complex had an apparent mass near 130 kDa. Enol was efficiently hydrated; aged material accumulated a resistant keto pool and an unidentified decay product. Hydratase kinetic values apply to the stated buffer/metal regime. Recombinant decarboxylase alone was unstable, whereas recombinant XylJ alone retained activity. Decarboxylase preferred the keto diacid and yielded predominantly the dienol used by hydratase. Hydrolytic formation of the dienol is attributed to Duggleby/Williams1986; hydrolase/hydratase separation was unpublished, and the hydratase product tautomer could not be determined. Isomerase also ketonized the five-carbon dienol in vitro; its principal oxidative-branch assays were buffer-sensitive. Decarboxylase kinetic values depended on how its keto substrate was prepared. [PMID:2681159]

Evidence scope: indexed abstract only. NAH7 and pWW0 shared gene order and sequence similarity supporting an evolutionary relationship. [PMID:3481421]

Evidence scope: complete publisher-transformed text, 14 pages; no raw PDF or figures. Main experiments used A. vinelandii206; other named Azotobacter strains remain distinct experimental scopes. Crude, high-speed and chromatography fractions differed; NADH oxidase interfered with assays. Catechol cleavage consumed equimolar oxygen. Alternative-substrate oxidation did not distinguish one broad enzyme from multiple oxygenases. Induced NAD-dependent semialdehyde oxidation dominated; NADase exposed weak noninducible hydrolysis. Endogenous NAD recycling confounded omission controls. EDTA-trapped product was isolated and compared by melting point and spectra; historical labels do not establish modern intermediate geometry. Spontaneous spectral conversion and extract acceleration were distinguished; heat stability complicated attribution, while fractionation and induction supported catalysis. Partially purified preparations coupled decarboxylation/hydration; magnesium or manganese stimulated, EDTA inhibited. Aldolase fractions produced separately measured acetaldehyde and pyruvate; only42% of synthetic substrate reacted, without absolute stereochemical assignment. Measured upstream activities increased after benzoate growth; aldolase did not show comparable induction. The proposed six-step route ends at acetaldehyde/pyruvate. Hydration was not separately characterized; tautomerase physiological necessity remained unresolved. The full 1971 publisher-transformed text is now inspected; it supports the historical six-step route only, without direct proof of the seventh CoA-acylating step or exact modern stereoforms. [PMID:4325686]

Evidence scope: complete publisher-transformed text, 6 pages; numeric OCR limits; no raw PDF or figures. KT2440 hosted pWW0 derivatives; distinguish experimental host from plasmid origin. N-terminal sequencing reassigns the earlier benzaldehyde-active preparation to XylG. It oxidized catechol and4-methylcatechol cleavage products, but not the3-methyl product. XylG pH optima were8.3 for semialdehyde and9.6 for benzaldehyde. Semialdehyde kinetics were measured here; aldehyde and NAD kinetics came from earlier studies. Preserve separate assays. XylC was purified from thexylG-deletion host and lacked semialdehyde activity. Its tetramer, buffer inhibition and kinetic data do not describe XylG. XylG homodimer status cites1990 work; the1995 paper does not newly measure that assembly. Proposed active-site explanations remain interpretations. [PMID:7868591]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. XylF modification and mutagenesis support a serine-hydrolase triad and altered F108M behavior. This is evidence for the alternative hydrolytic branch, not an oxidative-route reaction or exact dienol geometry. XylF of the P. putida TOL system hydrolyzes ring-cleavage products of 3-alkyl catechols; sequence comparison, chemical modification and mutagenesis support a serine-hydrolase catalytic triad. F108M increased thermostability and changed substrate preference. [PMID:7890778]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. Preliminary recombinant CF600 tautomerase crystallography supported a hexamer rather than pentamer. This organism-specific result must not alone identify the mt-2 assembly. [PMID:7966298]

Evidence scope: complete scientific main text from publisher transformation; no raw PDF or figures. DmpF-expressing E. coli extracts formed acetyl-CoA from acetaldehyde/CoA/NAD; unrelated dmpQ control and native acetate-growth controls were distinct. Propionaldehyde was an alternate substrate. Phenol-grown CF600 DmpFG copurified; N termini identified DmpF and DmpG. Measured bands were 34.5/40 kDa, with inferred sequence masses 32.5/37.5 kDa. Apparent 148 kDa solution mass supported two of each subunit. Manganese stimulated aldolase; zinc inhibited; magnesium/calcium did not stimulate. NADH stimulated aldolase in delayed-addition controls. Direct NADH binding to DmpG or an allosteric transmission mechanism was not demonstrated. EDTA dialysis left basal aldolase activity; added manganese activation did not settle whether tightly bound metal was essential. Hydrolyzed S-lactone substrate gave incomplete pyruvate recovery. Aldehyde and NAD/NADP comparisons were assay-specific; alternate substrates must not become formal catechol-route products. Channeling, protection from toxicity and ATP benefit were proposals. Alternative acetaldehyde-metabolizing activities existed; failed detection of DmpG alone could reflect expression or assay sensitivity. A single Results sentence associates propionaldehyde with 3-methylcatechol, conflicting with abstract/discussion mapping to 4-methyl/3,4-dimethylcatechol. Preserve the internal inconsistency. Native CF600 purification and heterologous DmpF assays are distinct preparations. DmpF-expressing extracts produced acetyl-CoA from acetaldehyde and propionyl-CoA from propionaldehyde; unrelated-gene and acetate-growth controls had negligible products. One results sentence links propionaldehyde to 3-methylcatechol; abstract and discussion instead associate propionaldehyde with 4-methyl/3,4-dimethylcatechol and acetaldehyde with catechol/3-methylcatechol. Aldolase and acylating dehydrogenase copurified through five chromatographic steps and ammonium fractionation. Two bands were identified by N-terminal sequences as DmpF and DmpG; stain intensity is approximate. Gel filtration mass was compatible with two copies of each subunit; monomer/homodimer peaks were not detected. Storage and dilution effects differ for the two activities. Activity depended on pH and buffer. Added manganese stimulated aldolase; zinc inhibited; magnesium and calcium did not stimulate this preparation. NADH stimulated complex-associated aldolase activity, with weaker NAD+ stimulation. Delayed-addition controls separate stimulation from the lactate-dehydrogenase reporter. Direct allostery of DmpG and conformational signaling through DmpF were alternative explanations for nucleotide stimulation. Incomplete pyruvate recovery was attributed to substrate instability; equilibrium and a simple precursor impurity explanation were disfavored. Purified complex showed aldehyde and nucleotide preferences under one assay condition. Other acetaldehyde-metabolizing activities were present; failure to detect DmpG alone could reflect expression or assay sensitivity. Dmp decarboxylase/hydratase association was unpublished context, and channeling, toxicity protection and ATP benefit were proposals. [PMID:8419288]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. Structures distinguished hexameric 4-OT from trimeric CHMI. Their proposed common one-base mechanism and substrate specificity are structural interpretations; no transfer of CHMI stoichiometry to XylH. [PMID:8547259]

Evidence scope: complete scientific HTML main text and four visual figures. Nitrobenzene-grown JS45 deaminase was purified by sequential anion exchange, copper chelate, gel filtration and hydrophobic steps. Purified deaminase has16.6kDa subunits and apparent100kDa native mass; six identical subunits are inferred. These measurements are not4OT measurements. Crude extracts accelerate hydroxymuconate tautomerization (about7min to2min half-life at0.1mg/ml), whereas purified deaminase does not. Spontaneous conversion is measured in25mM phosphate pH8.0,0.15MNaCl. It is distinct from1971 conditions; no universal half-life is inferred. Rapid spectra support direct keto product rather than a detectable hydroxymuconate intermediate. The imine/proton-donor mechanism is an inference, not direct intermediate isolation. Tautomerase activity in JS45 extract need not participate in its aminophenol route; component presence does not prove catechol pathway execution. Metal effects, EDTA insensitivity and histidine-reagent inhibition describe the deaminase. Do not attach them to4OT. [PMID:9573204]

Evidence scope: complete abstract only; full primary paper not obtained. Inhibitor-modified 4-OT is described as a trimer of dimers. Pro1 and neighboring Arg39/Arg61 contacts support a mechanistic proposal, not a direct unmodified substrate-turnover measurement. [PMID:9778344]

AP3 names remain accession-specific: AB020521.1 CDS BAB03534.1 (6079–6864) is amnF hydratase, BAB03535.1 (6874–7644) is amnD decarboxylase and BAB03536.1 (7650–8078) is amnE deaminase in ENA. The 2000 indexed abstract instead gives AmnD hydratase/AmnE decarboxylase/AmnF deaminase. Current UniProt Q9KWS3 uses amnE for the exact BAB03535.1 sequence. Bare AmnD/E/F labels therefore cannot resolve these entities. Issuing deposit: https://www.ebi.ac.uk/ena/browser/view/AB020521.1; exact deposited CDS and translated sequence proof are retained in the source dossier. [UniProtKB:Q9KWS3; PMID:11081795]

The modern 8IH6 structure describes an engineered author/PISA assembly of five hydratase and five decarboxylase chains. The hydratase is ADLNW followed by the complete 261-residue Q9KWS4 sequence; the decarboxylase is AA followed by the complete 256-residue Q9KWS3 sequence. Deposit source taxon306 and E. coli expression host562 have distinct roles. This is separate from the historical database-reported 300 kDa preparation and 1:1 ratio; it does not prove the historical assembly had five copies of each. The deposit citation is still unpublished. [DOI:10.2210/pdb8ih6/pdb; UniProtKB:Q9KWS3; UniProtKB:Q9KWS4]

1BJP has five asymmetric-unit chains, while each of its three author/PISA biological assemblies has six instances. The sequence corresponds to Q01468 after removal of its initial methionine, and the Pro-1 inhibitor adduct defines a modified state. Neither five crystal chains nor the historical apparent pentamer overturns the six-member biological assembly for this deposited preparation. [DOI:10.2210/pdb1bjp/pdb; UniProtKB:Q01468; PMID:9778344]

Preserve these source wording/slot tensions until PMID7868591 checks. No NAD-exclusive claim. Native activity ENZRXN-3582 is retained at its stated inference level. Structured database context: physiologically-relevant true; ph-opt 8.3; alternative-substrate slot CPD-13339 → CPD-8781 (rejected as a product-replacement equation; original slot conflict retained); km 330.0 μM for NAD. These are source annotations, not universal optima, kinetic constants or primary-confirmed substrate equivalences. Primary assessment (PMID:7868591): Benzaldehyde and methyl semialdehydes are substrates; the native swapped product slot must not define new reaction chemistry. Primary preparation: XylG oxidized the catechol and 4-methylcatechol ring-cleavage semialdehydes; the 3-methylcatechol product was not oxidized. This preparation was reassigned from the earlier XylC attribution. No Km or error-sign normalization is accepted from ambiguous OCR; HMS pH optimum 8.3 differs from benzaldehyde optimum 9.6.
